Description: The naive Bayes algorithm is based on the Bayes’ theorem with the assumption of independence between each pair of features. It works well and can be used for both binary and multi-class categories in many real-world situations, such as document or text classification, spam filtering, etc. To effectively classify the noisy instances in the data and to construct a robust prediction model, the NB classifier can be used . The key benefit is that, compared to more sophisticated approaches, it needs a small amount of training data to estimate the necessary parameters and quickly. However, its performance may affect due to its strong assumptions on features independence. Gaussian, Multinomial, Complement, Bernoulli, and Categorical are the common variants of NB classifier.

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a linear decision boundary classifier created by fitting class conditional densities to data and applying Bayes’ rule. This method is also known as a generalization of Fisher’s linear discriminant, which projects a given dataset into a lower-dimensional space, i.e., a reduction of dimensionality that minimizes the complexity of the model or reduces the resulting model’s computational costs. The standard LDA model usually suits each class with a Gaussian density, assuming that all classes share the same covariance matrix. LDA is closely related to ANOVA (analysis of variance) and regression analysis, which seek to express one dependent variable as a linear combination of other features or measurements.

Another common probabilistic based statistical model used to solve classification issues in machine learning is Logistic Regression (LR) . Logistic regression typically uses a logistic function to estimate the probabilities, It can overfit high-dimensional datasets and works well when the dataset can be separated linearly. The regularization (L1 and L2) techniques  can be used to avoid over-fitting in such scenarios. The assumption of linearity between the dependent and independent variables is considered as a major drawback of Logistic Regression. It can be used for both classification and regression problems, but it is more commonly used for classification.

K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)  is an “instance-based learning” or non-generalizing learning, also known as a “lazy learning” algorithm. It does not focus on constructing a general internal model; instead, it stores all instances corresponding to training data in n-dimensional space. KNN uses data and classifies new data points based on similarity measures(e.g., Euclidean distance function) . Classification is computed from a simple majority vote of the k nearest neighbors of each point. It is quite robust to noisy training data, and accuracy depends on the data quality. The biggest issue with KNN is to choose the optimal number of neighbors to be considered. KNN can be used both for classification as well as regression.

In machine learning, another common technique that can be used for classification, regression, or other tasks is a support vector machine (SVM) . In high- or infinite-dimensional space, a support vector machine constructs a hyper-plane or set of hyper-planes. Intuitively, the hyper-plane, which has the greatest distance from the nearest training data points in any class, achieves a strong separation since, in general, the greater the margin, the lower the classifier’s generalization error. It is effective in high-dimensional spaces and can behave differently based on different mathematical functions known as the kernel. Linear, polynomial, radial basis function (RBF), sigmoid, etc
Decision tree (DT) is a well known non-parametric supervised learning method. DT learning methods are used for both the classification and regression tasks .

Thе ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3) algorithm is a classic decision tree algorithm used for both classification and regression tasks.ID3 deals primarily with categorical properties, which means that it can efficiently handle objects with a discrete set of values. This property is consistent with its suitability for problems where the input features are categorical rather than continuous.One of the strengths of ID3 is its ability to generate interpretable decision trees. The resulting tree structure is easily understood and visualized, providing insight into the decision-making process.

C4.5 is an effective technique for creating decision trees that can produce rules from the tree and handle both discrete and continuous attributes. The model’s accuracy is increased and overfitting is prevented by its utilization of gain ratio and decreased error pruning. Nevertheless, it might still be susceptible to noisy data and might not function effectively on datasets with a lot of features.

CART is a decision tree algorithm that can be used for both classification and regression tasks. CART can be used to create regression trees for continuous target variables in addition to classification. When deciding which subsets to split, the algorithm in this instance minimizes the variance of the target variable inside each subset.

BehavDT is a behavioral decision tree-based machine learning model designed to predict smartphone user activities by considering various contextual factors, such as temporal, spatial, and social contexts. Unlike traditional decision trees, BehavDT incorporates behavior-oriented generalization in both interior and leaf nodes, enabling it to capture diverse user behaviors in different situations. The model has been tested on real mobile phone datasets, demonstrating its ability to identify key decision nodes while capturing both general behaviors and specific exceptions. Although the model is demonstrated using phone call behaviors, it is applicable to other user-centric domains influenced by contextual factors.

IntruDTree is a machine-learning-based intrusion detection model designed to enhance security by prioritizing and ranking key security features based on their importance. The model uses these selected features to build an efficient tree-based intrusion detection system that reduces computational costs while improving prediction accuracy for unseen test cases. IntruDTree has been evaluated through experiments on cybersecurity datasets and compared against traditional machine learning methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting intrusions and optimizing security performance.

A random forest classifier is well known as an ensemble classifcation technique that is used in the field of machine learning and data science in various application areas. This method uses “parallel ensembling” which fits several decision tree classifiers in parallel, on different data set sub-samples and uses majority voting or averages for the outcome or final result. It thus minimizes the over-fitting problem and increases the prediction accuracy and control. Therefore, the RF learning model with multiple decision trees is typically more accurate than a single decision tree based model. To build a series of decision trees with controlled variation, it combines bootstrap aggregation (bagging) and random feature selection. Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) is an ensemble learning process that employs an iterative approach to improve poor classifiers by learning from their errors. Unlike the random forest that uses parallel ensembling, Adaboost uses “sequential ensembling”. It creates a powerful classifier by combining many poorly performing classifiers to obtain a good classifier of high accuracy. In that sense, AdaBoost is called an adaptive classifier by significantly improving the efficiency of the classifier, but in some instances, it can trigger overfits. AdaBoost is best used to boost the performance of decision trees, base estimator, on binary classification problems, however, is sensitive to noisy data and outliers.

Gradient Boosting, like Random Forests above, is an ensemble learning algorithm that generates a final model based on a series of individual models, typically decision trees. The gradient is used to minimize the loss function, similar to how neural networks use gradient descent to optimize weights. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) is a form of gradient boosting that takes more detailed approximations into account when determining the best model. It computes second-order gradients of the loss function to minimize loss and advanced regularization (L1 and L2), which reduces over-fitting, and improves model generalization and performance. XGBoost is fast to interpret and can handle large-sized datasets well.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is an iterative method for optimizing an objective function with appropriate smoothness properties, where the word ‘stochastic’ refers to random probability. This reduces the computational burden, particularly in high-dimensional optimization problems, allowing for faster iterations in exchange for a lower convergence rate.  In large-scale and sparse machine learning, SGD has been successfully applied to problems often encountered in text classification and natural language processing.

ZeroR is a simple classification algorithm that serves as a baseline model in machine learning. It predicts the most frequent class or value in the training dataset without considering any input features. ZeroR does not provide any insight into the data patterns but is often used to set a benchmark for evaluating the performance of more complex models. Its main purpose is to show how well a model can perform by just guessing the majority class, highlighting whether other algorithms offer meaningful improvements.

One-R (One Rule) is a simple and interpretable machine learning algorithm that creates a single rule for classification based on one feature. It evaluates each feature in the dataset and creates a rule that predicts the target class based on the most frequent class for each feature value. The feature with the lowest error rate is selected as the rule for the entire model. Although it is a basic algorithm, One-R often performs surprisingly well and serves as a baseline for evaluating more complex models.

DTNB (Decision Table Naive Bayes) is a hybrid machine learning algorithm that combines the strengths of two models: Decision Tables and Naive Bayes. It works by splitting the dataset into two parts: one is used to build a Decision Table (a rule-based classifier), and the other is used for Naive Bayes (a probabilistic classifier). DTNB aims to achieve better predictive performance by leveraging the rule-based approach's simplicity in handling structured data, along with Naive Bayes’ strength in probabilistic reasoning. This combination often results in a model that is both accurate and efficient.

Ripple Down Rule learner (RIDOR) is a rule-based machine learning algorithm that creates an ordered set of rules to classify instances. It starts by generating default rules to classify the majority class and then creates exceptions for misclassified instances. RIDOR refines the rules iteratively, adding exceptions and exceptions to exceptions as necessary, which allows it to handle complex datasets

Algorithm: Repeated Incremental Pruning to Produce Error Reduction (RIPPER)
Description: Repeated Incremental Pruning to Produce Error Reduction (RIPPER) is a rule-based machine learning algorithm designed for efficient classification, particularly on large datasets. It works by generating an initial set of rules from the training data, then incrementally refining and pruning these rules to reduce errors and improve generalization.

In this technique, the dependent variable is continuous, the independent variable(s) can be continuous or discrete, and the form of the regression line is linear. Linear regression creates a relationship between the dependent variable (Y) and one or more independent variables (X) (also known as regression line) using the best ft straight line .

Ordinary Least Squares regression (OLS) is a common technique for estimating coefficients of linear regression equations which describe the relationship between one or more independent quantitative variables and a dependent variable (simple or multiple linear regression), often evaluated using r-squared. Least squares stand for the minimum squares error (SSE). Maximum likelihood and Generalized method of moments estimator are alternative approaches to OLS

Stepwise regression is the step-by-step iterative construction of a regression model that involves the selection of independent variables to be used in a final model. It involves adding or removing potential explanatory variables in succession and testing for statistical significance after each iteration.

MARS (Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines) is a regression technique that models complex, nonlinear relationships by fitting piecewise linear regressions. It divides the data into regions and applies different regression functions within each region. MARS automatically selects and prunes these functions to prevent overfitting, making it a powerful tool for capturing nonlinear patterns while remaining interpretable.

LOESS (Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing) is a non-parametric regression technique that fits smooth curves to data by applying local weighted regression. It estimates the relationship between variables by fitting simple models, like linear or quadratic regressions, to small localized subsets of the data. The smoothing parameter determines how much of the data around each point is used for fitting, allowing LOESS to capture complex, nonlinear trends while maintaining flexibility. It's particularly useful for data where the relationship between variables changes over different regions.

Lasso regression algorithm works by obtaining the subset of predictors that minimizes prediction error for a response variable. This is achieved by imposing a constraint on data points and allowing some of them to shrink to zero value. The lasso regression is used to obtain the subset of predictors that helps in minimising the error in prediction. Lasso puts a constraint on the model parameters  that make the regression coefficients shrink to zero.

Ridge regression is a type of linear regression that incorporates regularization to prevent overfitting by adding a penalty term to the model. This penalty, also known as the L2 regularization, is the sum of the squared coefficients multiplied by a tuning parameter (lambda). By shrinking the regression coefficients toward zero, ridge regression reduces their variance, helping to improve model stability and performance, especially when dealing with multicollinearity or when the number of predictors exceeds the number of observations.

K-means clustering is a fast, robust, and simple algorithm that provides reliable results when data sets are well-separated from each other. The data points are allocated to a cluster in this algorithm in such a way that the amount of the squared distance between the data points and the centroid is as small as possible. In other words, the K means algorithm identifies the k number of centroids and then assigns each data point to the nearest cluster while keeping the centroids as small as possible. Since it begins with a random selection of cluster centers, the results can be inconsistent. Since extreme values can easily affect a mean, the K-means clustering algorithm is sensitive to outliers.

K-Medoids is a clustering algorithm similar to K-Means, but instead of using the mean to define cluster centers, it selects actual data points (medoids) as cluster centers. The medoid is the most centrally located point within a cluster, minimizing the sum of dissimilarities between itself and all other points in the cluster. K-Medoids is more robust than K-Means, especially when dealing with noise or outliers, because it minimizes a more general loss function that doesn't rely on averages. This makes K-Medoids effective in applications where using actual representative points is important.

CLARA (Clustering LARge Applications) is a clustering algorithm designed to efficiently handle large datasets. It is an extension of the K-Medoids algorithm and works by taking a representative sample of the data to form clusters. CLARA first randomly selects a subset of the data, applies the K-Medoids algorithm to find medoids, and then assigns the remaining data points to the nearest medoid. This process is repeated multiple times to ensure robustness, and the best clustering solution is chosen based on the overall quality of the clusters. CLARA is particularly effective for large datasets where traditional clustering methods may be computationally expensive or infeasible.

Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) is a base algorithm for density-based clustering which is widely used in data mining and machine learning. This is known as a nonparametric density-based clustering technique for separating high-density clusters from low-density clusters that are used in model building. DBSCAN’s main idea is that a point belongs to a cluster if it is close to many points from that cluster. It can find clusters of various shapes and sizes in a vast volume of data that is noisy and contains outliers. DBSCAN, unlike k-means, does not require a priori specification of the number of clusters in the data and can find arbitrarily shaped clusters.

Algorithm: Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure (OPTICS)
Description: OPTICS (Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure) is a clustering algorithm that extends DBSCAN by identifying clusters of varying densities without requiring predefined parameters. It organizes the data points into an ordering based on their reachability distances, capturing the cluster structure in a hierarchical manner. This allows users to visualize the clustering results and choose appropriate levels of clustering. OPTICS is effective for handling noise and outliers, making it suitable for complex datasets with varying densities

The STING (Statistical Information Grid) algorithm is a grid-based data mining technique that partitions the data space into cells, each containing statistical summaries like mean and variance. It efficiently reduces the dataset size, enabling quick statistical analysis and clustering. By allowing hierarchical query processing, STING can identify data density in different regions, making it suitable for large spatial datasets. Overall, it enhances computational efficiency while extracting meaningful patterns from data.

CLIQUE (Clustering In QUEst) is a clustering algorithm designed for high-dimensional data. It partitions the data space into overlapping hypercubes to identify dense regions containing a minimum number of points. By combining clustering with dimensionality reduction, CLIQUE effectively discovers clusters in high-dimensional datasets where traditional methods may struggle, making it useful for data mining and exploratory analysis.

Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) are often used for data clustering, which is a distribution based clustering algorithm. A Gaussian mixture model is a probabilistic model in which all the data points are produced by a mixture of a finite number of Gaussian distributions with unknown parameters. To find the Gaussian parameters for each cluster, an optimization algorithm called expectation-maximization (EM) can be used. EM is an iterative method that uses a statistical model to estimate the parameters. In contrast to k-means, Gaussian mixture models account for uncertainty and return the likelihood that a data point belongs to one of the k clusters. GMM clustering is more robust than k-means and works well even with non-linear data distributions.

COP K-means (Clustering of Partitions K-means) is a variation of the K-means algorithm that improves clustering quality by dividing the dataset into smaller partitions and applying K-means to each partition individually. This approach enhances efficiency and scalability, allowing for better handling of large datasets and potentially leading to improved clustering outcomes in complex data scenarios.

CMWK-Means (Clustered Multi-Weighted K-Means) is a variant of the K-means algorithm that incorporates multi-weighted data to improve clustering performance. By assigning different weights to data points based on their importance, CMWK-Means enhances the clustering results, especially in imbalanced or heterogeneous datasets, leading to more meaningful and accurate clusters compared to traditional K-means.

Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) is a dimensionality reduction technique that identifies linear relationships between a set of independent variables and one or more dependent variables. It transforms the original predictors into a smaller set of uncorrelated latent variables, which capture the most variance in the data. By projecting the data into this new space, PLSR effectively addresses multicollinearity and overfitting issues. It is widely used in fields like chemometrics and genomics for analyzing high-dimensional datasets

Sammon Mapping is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize high-dimensional data by preserving the pairwise distances between data points in a lower-dimensional space, typically two or three dimensions. Unlike linear methods like Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Sammon Mapping focuses on maintaining the structure of the data, making it effective for capturing complex relationships. The algorithm minimizes a stress function that measures the differences in distances between the original and lower-dimensional representations through iterative optimization. It is widely used in exploratory data analysis and pattern recognition to better understand and visualize intricate datasets.

Flexible Discriminant Analysis (FDA) is a classification method that extends traditional discriminant analysis by allowing for non-linear decision boundaries. Unlike linear models, FDA can capture complex relationships between predictor variables and class memberships using kernel methods. This flexibility makes FDA suitable for datasets where classes are not easily separable, enhancing classification accuracy in various applications, such as bioinformatics and marketing.

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) is a statistical classification technique that extends Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) by allowing for non-linear decision boundaries. Unlike LDA, which assumes that the predictors for each class share the same covariance matrix, QDA allows each class to have its own covariance matrix, resulting in a quadratic decision boundary. This flexibility enables QDA to model more complex relationships in the data, making it effective for classifying datasets where classes are not linearly separable. However, this increased flexibility also requires a larger sample size to estimate the covariance matrices accurately.

Mixture Discriminant Analysis (MDA) is a classification technique that combines mixture modeling with discriminant analysis, assuming that the data for each class comes from a mixture of probability distributions, typically Gaussian. This approach offers flexibility by accommodating multiple underlying distributions for each class, making it suitable for heterogeneous datasets. MDA uses methods like the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate parameters and provides a probabilistic framework for classifying observations based on the highest posterior probability. It is particularly effective in real-world applications where single distribution assumptions may not accurately represent class structures.

Regularized Discriminant Analysis (RDA) is a classification method that enhances traditional discriminant analysis by incorporating regularization to improve stability and prevent overfitting, particularly in small sample sizes or high-dimensional datasets. RDA offers flexibility by allowing a continuous trade-off between linear and quadratic decision boundaries through a regularization parameter. This approach helps to stabilize covariance matrix estimates, leading to improved generalization and classification performance. RDA is commonly used in fields like bioinformatics and finance, where robust classification in complex data scenarios is essential

Projection Pursuit is a statistical technique used for dimensionality reduction and data visualization that seeks to identify low-dimensional projections of high-dimensional data that reveal interesting structures or patterns. The method involves searching for optimal linear combinations of the original variables, known as projections, that maximize a specific criterion, often related to the non-normality or complexity of the projected data. By focusing on projections that highlight features like clusters or outliers, Projection Pursuit provides insights into the underlying structure of complex datasets.

Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) is a statistical technique used to visualize the similarities or dissimilarities among a set of objects in a lower-dimensional space, typically two or three dimensions. It starts with a distance matrix that quantifies the pairwise dissimilarities between objects and seeks to position them in such a way that the distances in the lower-dimensional representation closely reflect these original dissimilarities. There are two main types of MDS: classical MDS, which uses linear transformations, and non-metric MDS, which preserves the rank order of distances. MDS is widely applied in fields like psychology, marketing, and bioinformatics to explore and visualize complex datasets, helping to identify patterns and relationships.

AIS is the first algorithm for association rule mining. The AIS algorithm’s main downside is that too many candidate item sets are generated, requiring more space and wasting a lot of effort. This algorithm calls for too many passes over the entire dataset to produce the rules.

SETM (Set-based Association Rule Mining) is an algorithm designed for efficiently discovering association rules in large transactional databases by identifying frequently occurring itemsets. It employs a set-based approach, using data structures to represent itemsets, which allows for faster comparisons and computations compared to traditional methods. The algorithm reduces the number of transactions processed by maintaining a relevant subset, enhancing efficiency. After identifying frequent itemsets, SETM generates association rules and evaluates their strength using metrics like support, confidence, and lift, making it effective for applications such as market basket analysis.

The term ‘Apriori’ usually refers to having prior knowledge of frequent item set properties. Apriori uses a “bottom-up” approach, where it generates the candidate item sets. To reduce the search space, Apriori uses the property “all subsets of a frequent itemset must be frequent; and if an itemset is infrequent, then all its supersets must also be infrequent”. Another approach predictive Apriori can also generate rules; however, it receives unexpected results as it combines both the support and confdence.The Apriori is the widely applicable techniques in mining association rules.

Algorithm: Equivalence Class Clustering and bottomup Lattice Traversal (ECLAT)
Description: ECLAT uses a depth-frst search to fnd frequent itemsets. In contrast to the Apriori [8] algorithm, which represents data in a horizontal pattern, it represents data vertically. Hence, the ECLAT algorithm is more efcient and scalable in the area of association rule learning. This algorithm is better suited for small and medium datasets whereas the Apriori algorithm is used for large datasets.

Another common association rule learning technique based on the frequent-pattern tree (FP-tree) is Frequent Pattern Growth, known as FP-Growth. The key diference with Apriori is that while generating rules, the Apriori algorithm generates frequent candidate itemsets; on the other hand,the FP-growth algorithm prevents candidate generation and thus produces a tree by the successful strategy of ‘divide and conquer’ approach. Due to its sophistication, however, FP-Tree is challenging to use in an interactive mining environment . Thus, the FP-Tree would not fit into memory for massive data sets, making it challenging to process big data as well.

RARM (Rapid Association Rule Mining) is an algorithm focused on efficiently discovering association rules in large datasets while addressing performance challenges faced by traditional mining methods. It utilizes a sampling technique and a two-phase process to generate candidate itemsets from a sample and then verifies them against the entire dataset, significantly reducing the number of database scans needed. RARM is designed to optimize memory usage, making it suitable for environments with limited resources. This algorithm is particularly effective for real-time applications, such as market basket analysis, where quick and efficient rule discovery is essential.

This algorithm fIrst constructs an association generation tree (AGT), a top-down approach, and then extracts the association rules through traversing the tree.
